issues.legal_issue: A government’s lease of mineral land to another party does not infringe a former user’s fundamental rights merely because the former user had previously excavated minerals in the area.
material_facts: The government owned the land and its minerals.
The area leased to the third party did not include any portion previously leased to the petitioners.
The petitioners showed no legal authority giving them a right to have that area leased to them instead of to another party.
issues.conclusion: The grant of the lease did not infringe the petitioners’ fundamental rights or create the claimed monopoly.
issues.legal_principle: The government, as owner of land and its minerals, was prima facie entitled to lease them. Prior use, without a demonstrated legal right to the land or lease, did not establish a fundamental-rights violation or a monopoly. The Court relied on no earlier cases or specific constitutional provision for this conclusion.

rule.if: article_32_challenge_to_government_mineral_lease and government_owns_mineral_land and leased_area_not_previously_leased_to_petitioner and not petitioner_has_legal_right_to_lease_area

predicates.article_32_challenge_to_government_miner: A petitioner seeks constitutional writ relief against the government's grant of a mineral lease.
predicates.government_owns_mineral_land: The government owns the land and the minerals being leased.
predicates.leased_area_not_previously_leased_to_pet: The area granted to the new lessee was not part of an area previously leased to the petitioner.
predicates.petitioner_has_legal_right_to_lease_area: The petitioner has a legal right to have the area leased to them rather than to another party.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ challenges a government mineral lease, the government owns the mineral land, the leased area was not previously leased to the petitioner, and the petitioner has no legal right to that lease, the grant does not infringe the petitioner's fundamental rights.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that government action is illegal does not make a petition under Article 32 maintainable unless the action violates a fundamental right.
material_facts: The petitioners challenged the government’s grant of a mineral lease as illegal under mining legislation and rules.
The Court found no fundamental right infringed by the grant of the lease.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming the grant was illegal, the petitioners could not obtain relief under Article 32 without a violation of a fundamental right.
issues.legal_principle: Article 32 relief requires a violation of a fundamental right; alleged illegality by itself is insufficient. The Court relied on Article 32 and cited no earlier cases for this principle.

rule.if: article_32_petition and government_action_alleged_illegal and not fundamental_right_violated

predicates.article_32_petition: The proceeding is a petition seeking relief under the constitutional remedy for enforcement of fundamental rights.
predicates.government_action_alleged_illegal: The petitioner alleges that government action is illegal.
predicates.fundamental_right_violated: The challenged action violates a fundamental right of the petitioner.

issues.definition: An Article 32 petition alleging illegal government action is not maintainable when that action violates no fundamental right.

issues.legal_issue: A lease of limestone is not shown to be subject to the rules for minor minerals merely because limestone used for lime burning is defined as a minor mineral.
material_facts: The lease described the subject as limestone but did not state that it was to be used for lime burning.
Limestone can be used for purposes other than lime burning.
The record provided no basis for finding that the limestone was used only for lime burning.
The Mineral Concession Rules, 1949 applied to the lease if the mineral was not a minor mineral; the local rules for minor minerals had not yet been framed when the lease was granted.
issues.conclusion: The lease was not shown to concern a minor mineral, so the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949 applied and the grant could not be held illegal on the asserted ground.
issues.legal_principle: The Mineral Concession Rules, 1949 defined minor minerals to include limestone used for lime burning, and Rule 4 excluded minor minerals from those rules, leaving their extraction to provincial rules. Section 4 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948 prohibited mining leases contrary to the applicable rules. Because the lease did not specify lime-burning use and the record did not establish that use, the Court held that the 1949 Rules applied. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: article_32_challenge_to_mining_lease and lease_describes_limestone and not lease_limits_limestone_to_lime_burning and no_evidence_limestone_only_used_for_lime_burning

predicates.article_32_challenge_to_mining_lease: The proceeding is a constitutional writ challenge to the grant of a mining lease.
predicates.lease_describes_limestone: The lease identifies limestone as the mineral being extracted.
predicates.lease_limits_limestone_to_lime_burning: The lease restricts the limestone to use for lime burning.
predicates.no_evidence_limestone_only_used_for_lime: The record contains no evidence that the limestone is used only for lime burning.

issues.definition: In a constitutional writ challenge, when a lease describes limestone but does not restrict it to lime burning and the record does not establish exclusive lime-burning use, the minor-mineral challenge to the lease fails.

issues.legal_issue: A claim arising from the closure of mineral-processing premises does not sustain current Article 32 relief after the relevant permission has expired, and expiry does not establish a right to renewal.
material_facts: The petitioners alleged that they had been ordered to close their lime-kilns during the term of their permission or lease.
The petitioners’ own account placed the end of the relevant term on July 31, 1955, so no term remained in force when the Court considered the petitions.
The document relied on by the petitioners described a request for permission for non-agricultural use and did not establish that they held a lease rather than a licence.
The document required an application for renewal before expiry but did not promise renewal or establish a right to renewal.
The respondents disputed that the petitioners had held a lease.
issues.conclusion: The closure-related aspect of the petitions was infructuous after the term ended; any claim for damages or other relief could be pursued separately. The petitioners also failed to establish a lease or a right to renewal.
issues.legal_principle: An expired permission or lease does not establish an ongoing right supporting the requested constitutional relief. A requirement to apply for renewal does not itself confer a right to renewal, and the Court found the evidence insufficient to establish that the petitioners held a lease rather than licences. The Court relied on Article 32 and the terms of the document in evidence, and cited no earlier cases.

rule.if: article_32_claim_about_closure_of_business_premises and relevant_term_expired and not current_authorization_exists and not evidence_establishes_right_to_renewal

predicates.article_32_claim_about_closure_of_busine: The proceeding seeks constitutional writ relief for government-ordered closure of premises used in the petitioner's business.
predicates.relevant_term_expired: The term of the permission or lease connected with the premises has ended.
predicates.current_authorization_exists: The petitioner still holds a current permission or lease for the premises.
predicates.evidence_establishes_right_to_renewal: The evidence establishes that the petitioner has a right to renewal of the permission or lease.

issues.definition: When an Article 32 closure claim concerns premises whose relevant term has ended, no current authorization exists, and the evidence establishes no right to renewal, the closure claim is infructuous and no renewal right is established.
